summary: The Diameter base protocol is designed to be extended with new applications. This Best Current Practice document is a companion that explains when to define a new application versus extend an existing one, and gives guidance on designing Diameter applications and their extensions.

eli5.summary: Diameter is a system for network gear to ask who may do what. This guide tells people building new add-ons how to design them well, and when to change an old one rather than make a new one.

questions: how to design a diameter application
when to define a new diameter application
subtitle: Rules and design advice for extending Diameter without breaking the peers that already speak it.

tldr.problem: Diameter can be extended with new commands, AVPs and applications, but careless extensions break older nodes and cause interoperability failures.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC clarifies the base protocol's extension rules and gives guidelines: reuse as much as possible, treat mandatory (M-bit) additions as new applications, prefer extensible AVP types over Enumerated, and register values properly.
tldr.outcome: It is a Best Current Practice (BCP 193) companion to the Diameter base protocol that application designers are expected to follow when reusing or defining Diameter applications.

today: RFC 7423 is a Best Current Practice (BCP 193) and has not been obsoleted or updated, so it remains the guidance for designing Diameter applications. It builds on RFC 6733.

sections.title: Why Extension Rules Need Guidance
sections.content:
The Diameter base protocol (RFC 6733) provides an Authentication, Authorization, and Accounting (AAA) framework. Peers exchange messages that carry data as Attribute-Value Pairs (AVPs). The base protocol lets you extend it, and RFC 6733 sets rules for when an extension needs a new application identifier or a new command code.

This document does not change those rules. It clarifies them, discusses design choices and presents trade-offs. It names four kinds of extension: adding functionality to an existing application without a new one, adding functionality that does require a new application, defining an entirely new application, and defining a generic functionality reusable across applications.
sections.eli5: Diameter has rules for adding new features. This guide explains the rules in plain terms so builders do not accidentally break things that already work.

sections.title: Reuse First, and Minor vs Major Extensions
sections.content:
The RFC describes Diameter as two layers. The lower layer manages connections between neighbouring peers and routes messages. The upper layer is where applications live. Its main guiding principle for designers is: try to reuse as much as possible. Reuse shortens the specification work, reduces implementation effort and reduces testing. Reuse is not appropriate when the existing functionality does not fit or would lead to ambiguity.

Extensions fall into two groups. A minor extension adds optional features and has no backward-compatibility issue; a typical example is a new optional AVP in an existing command, which nodes that do not know it simply ignore. A major extension requires a new Diameter application because it breaks compatibility, for example a new command or a new AVP carried with the M-bit set.
sections.eli5: Adding an optional sticker to a form is harmless, because people who do not care can ignore it. Adding a required box changes the form, so you need a whole new form.

sections.title: Reusing Existing Applications
sections.content:
Adding a new command to an existing application is a major extension and needs a new application. A node that does not know the command would reject it with the protocol error DIAMETER_COMMAND_UNSUPPORTED and the transaction would fail. Deleting a command likewise requires a new application. The RFC warns that importing commands too liberally can produce a monolithic, hard-to-manage application.

For AVPs, the key is the M-bit. A mandatory AVP (M-bit set) MUST NOT be added to an existing command without defining a new application. Before choosing the M-bit, designers should ask whether the receiver must understand the AVP, whether it changes the state machine or the number of round trips, whether it separates incompatible variants, or whether it has a dual meaning. A single yes means the M-bit MUST be set and a new application MUST be defined.

Optional AVPs have pitfalls too: AVPs with intersecting meaning, AVPs with a dual purpose, and optional AVPs of which the text says at least one must be understood, which is really a mandatory AVP in disguise.

When deleting AVPs from a command, the RFC advises reusing the command syntax unchanged and ignoring, not deleting, optional AVPs that are not needed. Flag changes are limited: a mandatory AVP MAY be turned optional, but an optional AVP MUST NOT become mandatory without a new application. For reused Enumerated AVPs, it is RECOMMENDED not to change the set of valid values; define a new AVP instead.
sections.eli5: If you add a must-understand rule, everyone has to upgrade together, so it needs a new version. Optional extras are fine because anyone can skip them. Do not remove or rename things that others rely on.

sections.title: Defining New Applications and Commands
sections.content:
When requirements cannot be met by existing applications, a new one is justified; the RFC cites the 3GPP IP Multimedia Subsystem interfaces Cx/Dx and Sh as examples. Designers SHOULD import existing AVPs and AVP values for new commands, and SHOULD NOT define commands from scratch: start from an existing command with similar functionality.

The command syntax should favour extensibility. Defining most AVPs as optional is considered a good design choice in many cases, and the designer MUST state why optional AVPs may be present or absent and how nodes behave when they are absent. Adding a wildcard entry for any number of optional AVPs (written asterisk, space, [AVP]) to the command syntax allows arbitrary optional AVPs with the M-bit cleared.

Session-level messages (RAR/RAA, STR/STA, ASR/ASA, and possibly ACR/ACA in the coupled accounting model) SHOULD carry the new application's own Application Id, to avoid routing problems. Designers SHOULD NOT use the Vendor-Id AVP to differentiate vendor-specific Application Ids, since Diameter routing is not based on Vendor Id.
sections.eli5: When building something new, copy a part that already works and tweak it. Make most fields optional so the design can grow, and stamp every message with the right application label so it gets delivered.

sections.title: Enumerated AVPs and Better Alternatives
sections.content:
AVPs of type Enumerated have a fixed list of valid values that cannot be changed in practice without backward-compatibility problems. The RFC says Enumerated AVPs MUST NOT be extended by adding new values. If growth is foreseen, it is RECOMMENDED to use Unsigned32 or Unsigned64 instead, so the value space (0 to 2^32 - 1 or 0 to 2^64 - 1) is valid at the base protocol level and only clients and servers interpret it.

The RFC illustrates this with an Access-Network-Type AVP whose thousands digit gives the class (1xxx mobile, 2xxx fixed, 3xxx wireless). Enumerated AVPs are also often misused as simple Boolean flags. Designers SHOULD instead use an unsigned AVP as a bit mask that leaves room for future additions, like the Session-Binding AVP in RFC 6733.
sections.eli5: A multiple-choice list with a few fixed answers is hard to add to later. A numbered shelf with lots of empty slots lets you put new things in without rebuilding it.

sections.title: Sessions, Routing, Translation and Accounting
sections.content:
Sessions. If an application relies on base-protocol session management, its commands MUST include the Session-Id AVP. If not, Auth-Session-State MUST be included and set to NO_STATE_MAINTAINED, and the documentation MUST say how sessions are handled.

Routing. Some applications need to route on the User-Name or other AVPs rather than just Destination-Realm and Application Id; such mechanisms MUST be described in the application documentation, typically through an application-specific proxy agent. Answers MUST follow the reverse path of the request, and designers MUST NOT modify the answer-routing principles of RFC 6733.

Translation. Designers SHOULD NOT assume a standard Diameter-to-RADIUS gateway exists; RADIUS translation material was removed in RFC 7155, so the required translation SHOULD be specified with the application.

Accounting. Two models are given: split (uses the base accounting Application Id, value 3, and can be routed to a central accounting server) and coupled (uses the application's own Application Id). The coupled model is RECOMMENDED for most cases. Designers SHOULD NOT define new commands for application-specific accounting records.
sections.eli5: Every conversation needs a way to be tracked, letters need to be routed to the right office, and the bill can either go to a central billing desk or stay with the shop that did the work.

sections.title: Registering Diameter Values
sections.content:
The RFC summarises how to register each kind of extension with IANA. New AVP values need guidance on the policy for adding more; for example, new Result-Code values go through IETF Review. AVP codes live either in the IETF namespace (assigned after Expert Review, or IETF Review for a block) or in a vendor-specific namespace based on a private enterprise number in the Vendor-Id field; Vendor-Id zero or absent means the IETF namespace.

The Command Code namespace is flat but divided into standard values (IETF Review), vendor-specific values (first-come, first-served) and a range for experimentation and testing. The Application-Id namespace is divided into standard values (Expert Review) and vendor-specific values (first-come, first-served). When more than one vendor uses the same extension, a standard extension is RECOMMENDED.
sections.eli5: Names and numbers for new features go in an official list so two companies do not pick the same one. Some slots need careful review, and some are given out in the order people ask.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The document gives no new security guidance, but extensions SHOULD NOT break the security concept of RFC 6733. Any command defined or reused in a new application SHOULD be secured with TLS or DTLS/SCTP and MUST NOT be used without one of TLS, DTLS or IPsec. Any impact on existing security principles MUST be assessed and documented in the application specification.

When IPsec is used between peers, ESP in transport mode with non-null encryption and authentication MUST be used, and IKEv2 SHOULD be used for mutual authentication and security associations.
sections.eli5: New add-ons must keep the locks the system already has. Messages between servers have to travel in a protected tunnel.
